results.title: Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Models in R and Python with GPBoost | Towards Data Science
results.content: # Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Models in R and Python with GPBoost. **GPBoost is a recently released C++ software library that, among other things, allows for fitting generalized linear mixed effects models in R and Python**. Generalized linear mixed effects models (GLMMs) assume that a response variable *y* follows a known parametric distribution *p(y|mu)* and that a parameter *mu* of this distribution (often the mean) is related to the sum of so-called fixed effects *Xb* and random effects *Zu*:. Further, random effects can consist of Gaussian processes used, for instance, for modeling spatial data. Compared to using fixed effects only, random effects have the advantage that a model can be more efficiently estimated when, e.g., the number of groups or categories is large relative to the sample size. pred = gp_model.predict(X_pred=X_test, group_data_pred=group_test, predict_var=True, predict_response=False) print(pred['mu']) # predicted latent mean print(pred['var']) # predicted latent variance. pred <- predict(gp_model, X_pred=X_test, group_data_pred=group_test, predict_var=TRUE, predict_response=FALSE) pred$mu # predicted latent mean pred$var # predicted latent variance. If `group_data_pred` contains new, unobserved categories, the corresponding random effects predictions will be 0. In detail, we vary these choices as follows: (1.) number of samples: 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, (2.) number of groups: 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, (3.) number of covariates: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, (4.) nested and crossed random effects models, and (5.) a Poisson likelihood instead of binary one. For instance, for a binary single-level random effects model with 100 groups, 1000 samples, and 20 covariates, `gpboost` is on average approximately 600 times faster than `lme4`. GPBoost is a recently released C++ software library that, among other things, allows for fitting generalized linear mixed effects models in R and Python. Besides grouped random effects considered in this article, GPBoost also allows for modeling Gaussian processes for, e.g., spatial or temporal random effects, as well as combined grouped random effects and Gaussian process models. Finally, apart from LMMs and GLMMs, GPBoost also allows for learning non-linear models without assuming any functional form on the fixed effects using tree-boosting; see these two blog posts on combining tree-boosting with grouped random effects and Gaussian processes or Sigrist (2020) and Sigrist (2021) for more details.

results.title: r - Mixed effects model with random and nested effects in lmer - Cross Validated
results.content: # Mixed effects model with random and nested effects in lmer. I want to run a linear mixed effects model with nested and random effects using lmer in R, but continue getting errors. Two questions: what is causing the errors and how can I fix my model to run the appropriate analyses? **Experimental design:** Four sites- each site has 2 plant species and 3 accessions for each plant species (6 accessions total). I also set Accession (coded 1 - 6), Site (coded 1 - 4), and SoilN treatment (coded 1 and 2) as factors. **Model:** I want to test the effects of treatment (SoilN), Species, and Accession on plant growth and root traits. I have been running two models- one for species and one for accession. I would like to test an interaction between species or accession and soil N, include site as a random effect, and nest accession within species. For the accession model (lf2), I get the following warnings:. 1. The model runs if I nest `Accession` within `Species` within `Site`, although I'm not sure that's a correct way to analyze the data. 2. It also runs if I don't nest `Accession` within `Species`, but still include `Site` and `Accession` as random effects. * $\begingroup$ You cannot have `Species` as both a fixed effect and a random effect. Try `LogLeaf ~ SoilN * Species + (1|Site/Accession)`. A few questions: What are "accessions"? * $\begingroup$ @amoeba it isn't the case that a fixed effect can't also be random. An effect can be split into the fixed part (i.e., the average coefficient) and the random part (i.e., the variance around that average coefficient). We also want to make sure that the effect of accession and treatment differ by site, so I would specify this model: `LogLeaf ~ SoilN * Accession + (1 + SoilN + Accession|Site)` $\endgroup$.
